questions.question: In the $M^B/M/1$ queue, jobs arrive in batches and service times are i.i.d. $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$. What happens when a batch of $k\ge2$ jobs reaches the head of the queue and the single server becomes free?
options: The server serves all $k$ jobs together in one $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$ service time.
The whole batch moves to the server, which serves its $k$ jobs one after another.
Each of the $k$ jobs starts at once, and the batch leaves after its longest service.
The server serves one job of this batch, then one job of each later batch in turn.

questions.question: In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, $L(t)$ is the number of jobs in the system at time $t$. How does a sample path of $L(t)$ change at arrival and departure events?
options: It rises by one at each job arrival and falls by one at each departure.
It rises by the batch size at an arrival and falls by the batch size when a batch is done.
It jumps up by the batch size at an arrival and down by one at each departure.
It jumps up by the batch size, then decreases continuously while the batch is served.

questions.question: In the $M^B/M/1$ queue, batches arrive as a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_B$. Let $\pi(n)$ be the long-run fraction of arriving batches that see $n$ jobs and $p(n)$ the long-run fraction of time with $n$ jobs. Which statement is correct?
options: $\pi(n)=p(n)$, because the batches form a Poisson process and PASTA applies to them.
$\pi(n)=p(n)$ only if the batch size is constant, since random sizes break PASTA.
$\pi(n)\ne p(n)$ in general, because an arriving batch brings several jobs at once.
$\pi(n)=p(n)$ holds only after $\pi$ is shifted by $\mathbb{E}[B]$ to count the new jobs.

questions.question: In the $M^B/M/1$ queue, why is the number of jobs $L(t)$ enough to describe the state, without recording how long the job in service has already been served?
options: Batches arrive as a Poisson process, so the elapsed service time carries no information.
The load satisfies $\rho<1$, so the system empties regularly and forgets its past.
Batch sizes are i.i.d., so the jobs still to be served do not depend on the past.
Service times are exponential, so the remaining service time is again $\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)$.

questions.question: In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, batches arrive at rate $\lambda_B=1.5$ per hour, $\mathbb{P}(B=1)=\mathbb{P}(B=4)=1/2$, and the mean service time per job is $\mathbb{E}[S]=12$ minutes. What is the load $\rho$?

In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, $\mathbb{P}(B=1)=0.2$, $\mathbb{P}(B=2)=0.5$, $\mathbb{P}(B=3)=0.3$. A batch arrives and sees $m=1$ job. What is the probability that it up-crosses level $3$, that is, takes the number of jobs from at most $3$ to at least $4$?
options: $\mathbb{P}(B\ge2)=0.8$
$\mathbb{P}(B\le2)=0.7$

questions.question: An $M^B/M/1$ queue is empty just before time $0$. A batch of $4$ jobs arrives at time $0$, a batch of $2$ jobs at time $0.3$, and the first job completes service at time $0.8$; nothing else happens before time $1$. At time $1$, what are $L_s^B$ (jobs of the batch at the server) and $Q^B$ (batches in queue)?
options: $L_s^B=3$ and $Q^B=1$
$L_s^B=1$ and $Q^B=1$
$L_s^B=3$ and $Q^B=2$
$L_s^B=4$ and $Q^B=1$

questions.question: An $M^B/M/1$ queue is empty when a batch of $2$ jobs arrives at time $0$; their service times are $1.0$ and $0.5$. The next batch arrives at time $0.6$. How long does this second batch wait before it moves to the server?
In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, $\lambda_B=1$, $\mu=4$ and $\mathbb{P}(B=1)=\mathbb{P}(B=2)=1/2$. Using the level-crossing equation for $n=0$ and $\pi(0)=1-\rho$, what is $\pi(1)$?

In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, batches arrive as a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_B$ and every batch contains exactly $2$ jobs. Which statement about the arrival process of the individual jobs is correct?
options: It is Poisson with rate $2\lambda_B$, since doubling the counts of a Poisson process keeps it Poisson.
It is Poisson with rate $2\lambda_B$, since it superposes two Poisson streams of rate $\lambda_B$.
It is not Poisson, because the job rate $2\lambda_B$ differs from the batch rate $\lambda_B$.
It is not Poisson, because the two jobs of each batch arrive at exactly the same instant.

questions.question: An $M/M/1$ queue and an $M^B/M/1$ queue have the same job arrival rate $\lambda=\lambda_B\mathbb{E}[B]$ and the same service rate $\mu>\lambda$. How does the mean number of jobs $\mathbb{E}[L]$ compare?
options: It is larger in the batch queue unless every batch has one job, as batch jobs wait for each other.
It is equal in both, because both queues have the same load $\rho=\lambda/\mu$.
It is smaller in the batch queue, because there are fewer arrival events per hour.
It is larger only for random batch sizes; a constant size $B\equiv k$ gives the $M/M/1$ value.

questions.question: In the level-crossing equation of an $M^B/M/1$ queue with service rate $\mu$ and stationary probabilities $\pi(n)$, what is the long-run rate of down-crossings of level $n$, from $n+1$ to $n$ jobs?
options: $\mu\,\mathbb{E}[B]\,\pi(n+1)$, because a whole batch leaves the system at once.
$\mu\sum_{m>n}\pi(m)$, because any state above $n$ can drop below the level.
$\mu\,\pi(n+1)$, because jobs leave one at a time from state $n+1$ only.
$\mu\,\pi(n)$, because the down-crossing ends in the lower state $n$.

questions.question: In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, batches arrive at rate $\lambda_B=0.5$ per hour, $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.4$ hour, and $\mathbb{P}(B=1)=0.4$, $\mathbb{P}(B=2)=0.4$, $\mathbb{P}(B=3)=0.2$. What is the long-run probability that exactly $2$ jobs of a batch are at the server, $\mathbb{P}(L_s^B=2)$?

In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, batches arrive at rate $\lambda_B=1$ per hour, $\mathbb{P}(B=1)=\mathbb{P}(B=3)=1/2$ and $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.2$ hour. What is the long-run mean number of jobs of the batch at the server, $\mathbb{E}[L_s^B]$?

In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, $\lambda_B=2$ per hour, $B$ is uniform on $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\mu=20/3$ per hour, so that $\pi(0)=0.4$ and $\pi(1)=0.12$. What is the long-run rate of up-crossings of level $1$, from at most $1$ job to at least $2$ jobs?
options: $0.773$ per hour
$0.24$ per hour
$0.507$ per hour
$1.04$ per hour

questions.question: An $M^B/M/1$ queue has load $\rho=\lambda_B\mathbb{E}[B]\mathbb{E}[S]=0.6$, and its batch size has finite mean $\mathbb{E}[B]$ but $\mathbb{E}[B^2]=\infty$. Which statement about this queue is correct?
options: $\rho$ is in fact infinite, because the load depends on the second moment of $B$.
$\mathbb{E}[L]$ is finite, because $\rho<1$ on its own keeps every mean queue length finite.
$\mathbb{E}[L_s^B]$ is infinite, so the mean number in the system $\mathbb{E}[L]$ is infinite too.
$\mathbb{E}[L_s^B]$ is finite, at most $\mathbb{E}[B]$; only the queue part $\mathbb{E}[Q^B]$ can blow up.

questions.question: An $M/M/1$ queue and an $M^B/M/1$ queue with $\mathbb{P}(B\ge2)>0$ have the same load $\rho<1$. Which long-run quantity is equal in both queues for every such batch-size distribution?
options: The probability of exactly one job in the system, $\rho(1-\rho)$.
The time-average number of jobs at the server, equal to $\rho$.
The probability of at least two jobs in the system, $\rho^2$.
The fraction of time the server is idle, equal to $1-\rho$.

questions.question: In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, every batch has exactly $2$ jobs, $\lambda_B=1$ and $\mu=5$. Running the recursion $q(n+1)=\frac{\lambda_B}{\mu}\sum_{m=0}^{n}q(m)G(n-m)$ from $q(0)=1$ and normalising, what is $\pi(2)$?

In an $M^B/M/1$ queue, $\lambda_B=0.5$ per hour, $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.5$ hour, and $\mathbb{P}(B=1)=0.2$, $\mathbb{P}(B=2)=0.5$, $\mathbb{P}(B=4)=0.3$. With $L_s^B$ the number of jobs of the batch at the server, what fraction of arriving batches find $L_s^B\ge2$?
